messages.subject: Re: Complete example
messages.body_plain:
On 8/2/12 11:49 AM, Marco wrote:> Hello,
 >
 > I am an Italian student currently working on for a Pharma company. I came to know about Stan and I started to read the
 > User guide and I found it really interesting. You are really doing a nice job.
 > I would love to make a presentation within the company and try to make a comparison with WinBugs.
 >  From the code available I've seen that there is the folder with the WinBugs examples, but after run some examples and
 > get the results, I do not know how to generate some plots within stan.
 > Do you have any code complete for make a nice comparison of Stan to WinBugs, with graphs and different times?

This is the wrong group for this discussion.
The stan-dev group is for those working on the
guts of implementing Stan.

This discussion should be on stan-users.  There's
a link on the lower lefthand corner of:

   http://code.google.com/p/stan/

We're still tweaking the language, so the manual
and syntax are about to change a little bit.

The results are currently being generated by the Stan
program in comma-separated value (CSV) notation.

What do you know how to use?  You can read CSV files
into Python, R or Matlab.  There are R interfaces to
WinBUGS (like R2WinBUGS) and to JAGS (R2jags).

For Stan, there's a very simple R wrapper that we've tested
on Mac OS X and Linux in the top-level r2stan_sys.R
file.  And we're about to release and document a much
richer and more tightly integreated interface.

Stan's strength will be in more complex models (like
ones with hierarchical covariance components) than BUGS.

You probably want to compare effective sample size
divided by time after both implementations have converged.

- Bob

messages.body_plain:
Here's a link to version Beta.2 of the Stan User's Guide
and Reference Manual:

   http://stan.googlecode.com/files/stan-reference-beta.2.pdf

We've been playing with the syntax for Stan variable
declarations.  And I've gone through and copy-edited
the manual and revised it with more descriptions.  There's
a new section on vectorization in the optimization chapter
in the user's guide.

Please let us know if you find any errors at this point.
It's easiest to do that via e-mail to this list or
directly to:

   mc.sta...@gmail.com

We'd also be happy to listen to any feedback you have on
what's confusing.

- Bob

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Local Level Model Issue
messages.body_plain:
The issue is that the model

------------
   data {
     int[0,] J; // number of days
     real y[J]; // Polls
   }
   parameters {
     real alpha[J];
     real[0,.1] tau;
   }
   model {
	alpha[1]~uniform(0,1);
	for(i in 2:J)
		alpha[i]~normal(alpha[i-1],tau);
	for(i in 1:J)
		y[i]~normal(alpha[i],0.01);
  }
---------------

tries to sample

    alpha[1] ~ uniform(0,1);

but doesn't constrain alpha[1] to fall between 0 and 1.

So what happens is that in initialization or when
randomizing momentum in each iteration, alpha[1] is going
outside its support in the 0 to 1 range, and thus
uniform() returns not-a-number (NaN).

Fix 1.
Put a different prior on alpha[1].

For instance,

   alpha[1] ~ normal(0,100);

If you just drop the sampling statement for
alpha[1], you implicitly have an improper uniform
prior on alpha[1].  Because alpha[1] is constrained
through the sampling statement for alpha[2] in the
loop, this might work.  In general, the posterior
must be proper.

Fix 2.
Define alpha[1] separately with a constraint.

   real<lower=0,upper=1> alpha_1;

and then make alpha one element shorter:

   real alpha[J-1];

and then you can sample

   alpha_1 ~ uniform(0,1);

We've changed the constraint syntax on you since
your first post.  This is probably the last syntax change
before the 1.0 release, and we'll try very hard to
maintain backward compatibility after that.

Then you'll need to change the rest of the model:

   for(i in 2:J)
	alpha[i]~normal(alpha[i-1],tau);
   for(i in 1:J)
	y[i]~normal(alpha[i],0.01);

to something where the new indexing is one less

    alpha[1] ~ normal(alpha_1,tau);
    for (i in 2:(J-1))
        alpha[i] ~ normal(alpha[i-1],tau);

    y[1] ~ normal(alpha_1,0.01);
    for (i in 2:J)
        y[i] ~ normal(alpha[i-1],0.01);

This kind of loop unfolding and consequent index
fiddling's a pain, but we don't have a way to
define a constraint on a single member of
an array.

An only slight less efficient alternative would be to
define a derived

    real<lower=0,upper=1> alpha_1
    real alpha_raw[J-1];

and then a transformed parameter

transformed parameters {
    real alpha[J];
    alpha[1] <- alpha_1;
    for (j in 2:J)
        alpha[j] <- alpha_raw[j-1];
}

Then you can use alpha as before.

- Bob

The fix is available as of now in the Git repository,
but it'll take some time to push through to RStan
and the source tarball.

We're really hoping to release the official 1.0
version next week (while it's still August!).
After that, we'll be tracking which bug fixes go in
which releases more closely.

(For the stan-dev x-post: The root cause was using a double
rather than the template parameter for accumulators and using
a double rather than promoting the template param for return
type. I also added unit tests and error handling for size
boundary issues, such as trying to take the sample mean
of a length zero vector or the sample variance of
a length one vector.)

- Bob

messages.subject: Truncated Latent Normal Sampler
messages.body_plain:
Hi, I have an ordered multivariate response, y[i,j], that i wish to model by introducing a latent response, t[i,j], on which i impose a set of (independent) normal priors  truncated by ordered cutpoints, c[j,k], where c[j,y[i,j] - 1] < t[i,j] <= c[j,y[i,j]] .  I choose this approach instead of employing the 'ordered_logistic' distribution because I will later generalize the implied normal link function by replacing the normal on t[i,j] with a mixture of normals.

Stan does not yet allow me to declare constraints on each of the t[i,j] based on the y[i,j] in the parameters block.   So i would declare them as unrestricted.  Then in the models block i would impose a set of truncated normal distributions on the t[i,j] with the left and right truncation points for each t[i,j] based on the values of  c[j] and y[i,j].   Do I need to perform a series of Jacobian adjustments to lp_ to account for the transformation of the t[i,j] from restricted/truncated to unrestricted for HMC sampling since i didn't declare the t[i,j] as restricted in the parameters block?  In particular, I think page 164 of the manual shows the form of the transform and adjustment from restricted to unrestricted performed by Stan for 2-sided range restrictions? Alternatively, does the employment of the truncated normal distributions on the t[i,j] in the model block effectively communicate the range restrictions on the t[i,j] such that Stan would automatically perform the jacobian adjustment to unrestricted.

Lastly, am I required to manually input initial values for "t" and "c" in order to ensure the sampler finds coherence to observed "y" on launch?

Thanks, Terrance

--

messages.subject: rand_normal doesn't exist
messages.body_plain:
Sorry.  My bad.

The error message that Andrew got below is right.
The doc is wrong.  So far, we haven't implemented rand_normal,
so this code won't work:

 >    generated quantities {
 >      real y_rep[J];
 >      for (j in 1:J)
 >        y_rep[j] <- rand_normal (0,1);
 >    }

It's the next feature I'm going to add, but it
may take a bit to push it through all 30 or
so distributions.   I laid some of the groundwork before
1.0.0, so it's not that much work from here.

Daniel's already working on vectorizations for the
rest of the probability functions, too.  When both are
done, it'll simplify the manual.   For now, I'm also
going to take Ben's advice of adding a table indicating
which probability functions have been vectorized.
(And to enrich the error messages indicating which
signatures ARE available.)

I'll take the references to it out of the manual,
which I'm about to update w.r.t. Andrew's other
comments.

This is the problem with a 200-ish page manual -- it's
hard to keep giving it a complete proofread.  I
should stick to never adding things to the manual
until I add them to the code.

- Bob
